ENQUÊTE – Des journalistes dénoncent les: INVESTIGATION – Journalists denounce pressure from pro-Israel group Honest Reporting Canada
Plusieurs journalistes canadiens ont con: Several Canadian journalists have spoken out about the pressure they say they face from the pro-Israel charity Honest Reporting Canada.
Honest Reporting Canada (HRC) est un org: Honest Reporting Canada (HRC) is a charity that publishes “Action Alerts” on its website to denounce what it considers “Anti-Israel Bias” in the media. Photo: La Converse illustration based on HRC screenshots.
Après plusieurs semaines de travail, des: After several weeks of work, hours of research, dozens of calls, emails and interviews, I’m presenting an investigation that sheds light on the pressure Honest Reporting Canada (HRC) puts on media outlets and journalists in Canada. You have probably never heard the name of this organization, which obtained charitable status in 2019. Yet it gets talked about a lot in media circles.
Lors de la conférence nationale annuelle: At the Canadian Association of Journalists (CAJ) annual national conference in late May 2024, a panel titled “Let’s talk about it: an open forum on Israel, Gaza and newsrooms” loosened tongues. I wasn’t in Toronto that day, but my La Converse colleagues told me that all it took was the mention of Honest Reporting Canada’s name for testimonies from targeted journalists to pile up. Some denounced the organization’s methods, saying they received hundreds of messages every time HRC criticized their work on its website or social media.
J’avais découvert l’existence d’Honest R: I had come across Honest Reporting Canada by chance on social media a few months earlier, but I hadn’t taken the time to look into it then. After listening to my colleagues, we finally decided together to investigate the organization, taking press freedom as our angle.
Mais je me suis vite rendu compte que, s: But I quickly realized that, while the stories had been shared spontaneously in the private setting of the CAJ’s annual conference, it was far less straightforward to ask these journalists to speak publicly. I was turned down dozens of times by professionals who are convinced that “we need to talk about it” but don’t want to risk being quoted, even anonymously. Admittedly, journalists are more used to being the ones holding out the microphone.
J’ai toutefois recueilli les propos de p: I did, however, gather the words of several journalists in Quebec and Ontario, and I want to thank them for their trust. This investigation could not have seen the light of day without them. I also approached the two organizations that represent journalists in Canada, which are speaking out about Honest Reporting Canada for the first time in this article.
Je déplore toutefois le fait que l’équip: I regret, however, that the Honest Reporting Canada team did not respond to any of my interview requests. The absence of the organization’s voice in this report is all the more regrettable because it is the very subject of this investigation.
<strong>Plusieurs journalistes canadiens: Several Canadian journalists have told La Converse about the pressure they say they face from the pro-Israel charity Honest Reporting Canada. They denounce online pressure campaigns that they say have targeted them more and more frequently since the start of a new cycle of violence in Gaza. An investigation.
7 octobre 2023 – il y a plus d’un an, de: October 7, 2023 – more than a year ago, coordinated attacks by Hamas killed 1,205 Israelis and took 251 hostages, 97 of whom are still being held to this day. Following the assault, Benjamin Netanyahu’s government tasked the Israeli army with “eliminating Hamas.” The operations carried out in the Gaza Strip have so far killed <l1>more than 42,000</l1> Palestinians. The situation is so grave that a <l2>UN Commission of Inquiry</l2> has concluded that Israel’s leadership is responsible for “war crimes and crimes against humanity,” and Hamas for “war crimes.”
Au Canada, à plus de 8 000 km de là, rés: In Canada, more than 8,000 km away, the echoes of this tragedy resonate. Here, some pro-Israel organizations are waging a different kind of war: a war over information. Among them, Honest Reporting Canada (HRC), registered as a charity since 2019, defines its mission this way: “Israel is at the heart of a battle for public opinion, waged primarily through the media. To ensure Israel is represented fairly and accurately, Honest Reporting monitors the media.” The organization targets journalists, experts and columnists, but also university students and professors.
Son directeur général, Mike Fegelman, es: Its executive director, Mike Fegelman, believes the Jewish community “wasn’t doing enough” to denounce anti-Israel bias, and says he wants to “create a digital army for Israel” in an interview with <l1>Thej.ca</l1>.
<strong>« Ils encouragent leurs milliers: “They encourage their thousands of followers to write to us”
Nombreux sont les journalistes qui souha: Many journalists want to share their experience with Honest Reporting Canada, as long as they are guaranteed anonymity. This shows how sensitive the subject is for these media professionals, who say they fear the consequences for their careers: being stigmatized, being harassed or being pulled off certain subjects after speaking out…
Après la parution d’un article sur une m: After publishing an article about a pro-Palestinian demonstration, Dan*, a journalist at a major Montréal daily, received several dozen emails. Every day, new messages disparaging his work are sent to him. “Honest Reporting’s method is to publish an article on their site with your name, your outlet and what they blame you for… They encourage their thousands of followers to write to us, and they also email your management asking for changes to the article. It’s an approach I don’t like at all, especially since the demands are unfounded. (...) It just adds to the stress when we’re trying to do our jobs,” says Dan. According to this well-established journalist, “their goal isn’t really to get changes made (to the articles, editor’s note), but to discredit the paper and the journalist by sharing it massively on social media.”
Une autre journaliste du même quotidien: Another journalist at the same daily is irritated: “I pay close attention to criticism when it comes from reputable sources who point out obvious errors in my copy, which I correct where warranted – which didn’t happen on the subject I was targeted for – but I tend to ignore criticism from such a marginal group defending radical opinions.” Yet it is becoming harder to ignore this pressure, which affects more and more media professionals across the country.
À Ottawa, un journaliste ciblé par Hones: In Ottawa, a journalist targeted by Honest Reporting who doesn’t want to take the “risk” of speaking on the record confides in an email: “I always respond to constructive, or at least polite, criticism that I receive. I question myself, and if, after the exchange with the person, but also with my editors or the colleagues whose outside opinion I ask for, I think I need to change my article, I’m happy to do so. It’s the same for most journalists,” says Sean*. “That can only work if people come to us or to a legitimate body before launching a defamatory vendetta that can damage our reputation, even if the accusations are false. It seems to me that before publicly accusing someone of antisemitism, and doing it as a pack, that’s the least one should do,” he insists.
Les médias sont également visés en tant: Media outlets are also targeted as entities. For example, Honest Reporting Canada calls The Breach a “so-called ‘independent media outlet’ that is anti-Israel” on its website on October 15. “This is part of Honest Reporting’s long-standing pattern [of attacks], baselessly smearing critics of Israel, but it won’t deter us from doing quality journalism,” says Martin Lukacs, editor-in-chief of The Breach. “It is distressing to see that they say they contacted government representatives to strip us of our eligibility for the small amount of public funding we receive. But since we do award-winning, credible journalism, we doubt their lobbying will have any impact,” he continues.
<em>Toronto Star, Globe and Mail, La Pre: Toronto Star, Globe and Mail, La Presse, Montreal Gazette, CBC, Le Devoir, Radio-Canada, Calgary Herald, CTV, City News, Edmonton Journal, National Post, The Guardian, Winnipeg Sun… Every day, Honest Reporting publishes between two and eight “Action Alerts” on its website, aimed at one or another of these news outlets. Print, radio, television: everything is scrutinized to “ensure Israel is represented fairly and reliably,” according to HRC’s website. The organization says it wants to “challenge anti-Jewish rhetoric, especially when antisemitism hides behind a mask of anti-Israel criticism.” Journalists are thus named on HRC’s website and identified with their photo, their outlet’s logo and the words “Action Alert.” HRC, which claims more than 60,000 members, urges them to write to the targeted authors or to their management. The journalists we spoke with compare this method to “propaganda,” also spread on HRC’s social media. “Since they stigmatized me publicly, gave out my email – and given all the messages I received – I don’t know what else they could do, so I prefer to remain anonymous. But I’m glad people are finally talking about it! I’ve heard a lot of colleagues complain about it, but nobody really dares to speak up against what they do,” says Helena*, a reporter for a television network in Quebec. A few months ago, Helena discovered that Honest Reporting Canada had published a post about a report she had done at a pro-Palestinian demonstration. “I knew it would happen one day… Before, their actions were rather limited, but since October 7, we’ve all seen a strong mobilization from them. Since I often cover these issues, I couldn’t escape it,” says the young woman with a sigh. Every hour, she receives new emails. “Some simply reuse the template Honest Reporting provides, but others are personalized with messages like: ‘Shame on you,’ ‘You’re spreading Hamas propaganda,’ ‘You should be fired immediately’...” the journalist says. “Seeing all that, I didn’t know what to do; I wondered if I had done something wrong, if I should have done it differently; it was unsettling for me. In the end, my colleagues reassured me that I had done good work and had nothing to blame myself for. Honest Reporting takes the smallest thing, twists it and throws fire on it, it’s so ridiculous... Because now, everything is antisemitic to them. Everything, really everything!” Helena says in exasperation. To verify her account, La Converse watched the report in question and read the article published by Honest Reporting Canada. HRC’s concerns focus on elements beyond the journalist’s control, such as a sign visible in the background bearing the word “Intifada,” or on the outlet’s editorial choices, notably the “newsworthiness” of covering a demonstration the organization deems “hateful.” But is it the role of a charitable organization to suggest to media outlets which events to cover or not? “If someone says there’s no public interest, they’d better hold on to their hats to prove it! Especially since this is an event happening in a public space, so it would be very, very, very difficult, even impossible, to prove there’s no public interest,” says Éric-Pierre Champagne, president of the Fédération professionnelle des journalistes du Québec (FPJQ). Helena has no intention of giving in to the pressure. “I think that if we want to do our job properly and regain the public’s trust, we have to stick to our ethical rules, and compromises aren’t possible. They want to silence Palestinians, and that’s not acceptable. It’s not acceptable for Palestinians, it’s not acceptable for Ukrainians, just as it’s not acceptable to go after Jews for any reason. It’s not acceptable for anyone! They’re trying to create fear and push their own priorities. And that shows how important it is for journalists to keep doing what they do,” she says. She says she is fortunately able to count on the support of her management, which has decided not to act on Honest Reporting Canada’s accusations for now. Management asked the journalist to forward every email she receives from the organization so it can respond in case of threats. In other newsrooms, however, things don’t always go as well.
« Quand ils ont lancé<l1> cette campagne: “When they launched <l1>this campaign</l1> against me, I had never heard of them. It was at the end of 2021, and my inbox was flooded with messages. I had to dig on my own to figure out it was Honest Reporting. In the end, it was a colleague who sent me their article,” recalls Iman Kassam, a video reporter who recently left CTV News.
En plus de 14 ans de carrière, elle assu: In more than 14 years in the profession, she says she has never experienced such relentlessness. She says she was all the more surprised because her video report had nothing to do with Israel. “It was a report on the Wet’suwet’en protests, which took place at the end of 2021. It had nothing to do with the Middle East; it was about Indigenous peoples, Indigenous land defenders,” explains Iman Kassam. So how did a demonstration for First Nations rights end up in HRC’s sights?
« En fait, une des personnes que j’ai in: “Actually, one of the people I interviewed was wearing a keffiyeh and an orange flag that read: ‘Every Child Matters.’ It was a visual symbol of support and respect for the first inhabitants of this country, and that’s what they hold against me,” the journalist says. Here is a transcript of what this demonstrator says in the video: “The least we can do is stay in solidarity with them and show people that this land is rightfully theirs and will always be theirs, no matter how many immigrants have come here and no matter how many years have passed.”
Dans sa publication de 2021, Honest Repo: In its 2021 post, Honest Reporting Canada describes the interviewee, a man, as a “pro-Palestinian, anti-Israel protester,” based solely on his appearance. But HRC’s intervention earned Iman Kassam several weeks of what she considers “online harassment.” Emails say, for example, that she “should be fired” or that “people like (her) shouldn’t exist.”
Honest Reporting Canada a publié, sur so: Honest Reporting Canada published on its website a screenshot of the video report in which Iman Kassam appeared, before it was edited by CTV News. Photo: screenshot.
Iman Kassam indique qu’après avoir solli: Iman Kassam says that after asking her superiors for help to find out the procedure to follow in dealing with all these messages, she was met with silence. “I sent them the campaign that had been launched against me and asked them to send the organization a cease-and-desist letter, because I felt this was not acceptable, especially since I had already been a victim of cyberharassment before from far-right youths – with no help from them then either – but I never got a response,” she says.
« Chaque fois qu’un courriel arrivait, j: “Every time an email arrived, I forwarded it to my managers. On several occasions, I asked my bosses at CTV News for four things: to send Honest Reporting a cease-and-desist letter; to have an open dialogue to find out whether there were rules against showing a keffiyeh or a Palestinian flag on television; to know whether they supported my report; and, fourth, to know whether it was possible to ask management to have a conversation about what was happening. Again, I never got a response.”
La journaliste affirme qu’elle a dû gére: The journalist says she had to handle the situation alone. “It’s frightening to feel that you’re going to have to go through this alone, on the pretext that it’s part of the job. No, it’s not part of the job! I’ve been a journalist for 14 years and I only experienced this kind of mass harassment at CTV News. It’s an occupational hazard, but the company has to take responsibility and protect its employees. In the end, the only thing they told me was that I could file a complaint, on my own of course!”
L’histoire ne s’arrête pas là, puisque p: The story doesn’t end there: several months after her video report aired, Iman Kassam discovered it had disappeared from the TV network’s website. “It was deleted overnight, you can no longer find it online. So the video was removed, the quotes were removed,” she says bitterly. “I was never informed, I was never asked whether it was acceptable, I was never asked whether it was what I wanted or what I needed, and I was never given the chance to rewrite it, even though I don’t see why I should have. It’s an incredible story… Everything was done in secret.”
Des recherches effectuées à l’aide de l’: Searches carried out with the <l1>Wayback Machine</l1> tool, a kind of archive library of web pages, allowed La Converse to confirm that significant changes had indeed been made on the CTV News site. The byline of the journalist, who made the report with a colleague, was removed, and all the passages of the video showing her or showing the demonstrator in the keffiyeh were also deleted. While it is hard to date these changes precisely, we can establish that they took place between November 28, 2021, the date the report was first published online, and January 18, 2022, the date of the first archive of the web page on which they appear. That is, only a few days after HRC launched its email campaign targeting the journalist.
Un coup dur pour celle qui travaillait t: It was a blow for the journalist, who was still working in the Montréal newsroom when she noticed. “In doing so, CTV not only breached its own correction and retraction policy, but also silenced the voices of Indigenous land defenders. Many cases of silencing and erasure have happened because of Honest Reporting. It’s incredibly unfair, and it really goes to the heart of our democracy,” she says.
Iman Kassam a depuis quitté CTV News pou: Iman Kassam has since left CTV News to do academic research on how Canadians in Generation Z assess the credibility of news and the trust it inspires. Contacted about the report removed from its site, CTV News management has not responded to our requests to date.
À Toronto, une autre journaliste a elle: In Toronto, another journalist also ran into trouble after being targeted by Honest Reporting. “Samira Mohyeddin is the host of Unforked, a national radio show that looks at the food we eat to reveal its cultural and political dimensions. She is a journalist, documentary filmmaker and producer of the award-winning show The Current on CBC Radio One. [...] For more than 16 years, Samira has co-owned and operated a restaurant and market in Toronto’s West Queen West neighbourhood with her brother and sister. It’s by combining her two passions, food and journalism, that she stays curious, well informed and well fed.” These few lines, gleaned from the Canadian public broadcaster’s website, sum up the career of the woman who resigned in November 2023.
« Vous parler aujourd’hui, c’est prendre: “Talking to you today is taking a risk, and I don’t think many of my colleagues will speak openly. But it’s important,” Samira Mohyeddin says plainly. She is one of only two journalists, along with Iman Kassam, who did not request anonymity for this investigation.
Elle a été visée par HRC dès 2018 pour u: She was targeted by HRC as early as 2018 over a debate show that brought together young Israelis and Palestinians to discuss the “path to peace.” “These were kids who were born into this conflict. They had never known anything other than the occupation, you know, and it was a wonderful discussion. In fact, we got messages from all over Canada, from people telling us how wonderful it was to hear Palestinians and Israelis talk to each other like that. But Honest Reporting Canada didn’t like it and sent emails to my bosses,” she recalls.
Puis, au cours de l’été 2021, c’est un é: Then, in the summer of 2021, an episode of the weekly podcast Unforked, hosted by Samira Mohyeddin, brought on a new wave of messages on social media. At the heart of the debate: hummus, the Middle Eastern dish whose star ingredient is the chickpea. Invited by the journalist, an Israeli university sociologist, a Palestinian actor, a young Lebanese-Canadian woman who got her hummus recipe from her grandmother and a Palestinian activist journalist who wrote a book on Gaza’s cuisine talk for nearly 30 minutes. The conversation covers their relationship to this popular dish, whose family recipe is passed down from generation to generation, their views on hummus variations with non-traditional flavours, and the disputes over who can claim authorship of hummus. In the last quarter of the podcast, the debate turns to the fact that Israel has declared hummus a national dish and to the political implications of such a move.
Sur son site internet, HRC publie la pho: On its website, HRC publishes journalist Samira Mohyeddin’s photo without her consent and identifies her outlet with the CBC logo. Photo: screenshot.
Le jour même, HRC lance une « alerte » e: That same day, HRC issued an “alert” and asked its subscribers to launch an email campaign. The organization claims that “the series portrayed Israelis as ‘colonialists’ and occupiers of indigenous Palestinian lands, responsible for the erasure of so-called historic Palestinian communities,” and faults the host for having “described the rebirth of Israel in 1948 as the ‘Nakba,’ an inflammatory and hateful term that means ‘catastrophe’ in Arabic.” According to the organization, “this CBC program denied Jewish independence in the land of Israel and described the creation of Israel as a catastrophe, rather than the miracle and blessing that it truly is.”
Des accusations que Samira Mohyeddin rej: Samira Mohyeddin rejects these accusations: “My show is about food. It’s not a news program where I have to be balanced, it’s a show about food! It was a bit absurd, but you know, that’s what Honest Reporting does, which has one of the most Orwellian names you could imagine, because honesty is probably the last thing that characterizes them!”
Dans un premier temps, la directrice pri: At first, CBC’s senior director of current affairs, Alison Broddle, replied to HRC that no mistake had been made. “We made sure that the Israeli and Palestinian points of view were represented by qualified guests who had the opportunity and the airtime needed to express their opinions and to openly agree or disagree with one another,” Alison Broddle says in the ombudsman’s report.
N’étant pas satisfait de cette réponse,: Not satisfied with this response, HRC then turned to CBC’s ombudsman, Jack Nagler, an independent mediator between the public broadcaster and its audience. In a <l1>detailed report</l1>, he found that “for a listener prepared by the introduction to learn more about the ‘debate’ (namely, the origin of hummus, Editor’s note), this was not balanced programming,” but he dismissed all the other grounds for complaint submitted by HRC, pointing out that the guests, who are not journalists, “were perfectly entitled to hold those opinions and make those statements.”
À propos du terme « <em>nakba</em> », l’: On the term “nakba,” the ombudsman stated the following: “This wasn’t Samira Mohyeddin describing the creation of Israel as a catastrophe. It was clearly an attempt to define a word that many listeners may not be familiar with. I believe CBC was right to do so.” Jack Nagler ultimately concluded that the episode violated CBC policy on the grounds that the way the topic was introduced could have led the audience to expect a different kind of debate.
« Si vous lisez le <l1>rapport</l1> de l: “If you read the ombudsman’s <l1>report</l1>, you’ll see that he doesn’t agree with any of their criticisms and that, at the end, he throws them a bone to calm them down. I didn’t like finding that out, I don’t think he was right in his assessment and I found it ridiculous,” Samira Mohyeddin insists.
De son côté, Honest Reporting Canada a q: For its part, Honest Reporting Canada called the decision a “victory” on its website and social media: “It is important to note that the ombudsman’s report testifies to the power and impact of Honest Reporting Canada’s subscribers, who denounce problematic coverage of anti-Israel events and who helped bring this problematic episode to the attention of CBC management.”

Samira Mohyeddin considère que ce genre: Samira Mohyeddin believes this kind of situation pushes some journalists toward self-censorship. “I left CBC, but it wasn’t because of this particular story. I left to do something else and I’m glad I’m not there right now because I wouldn’t be able to handle it. Today, I have the freedom to tell the truth, which is far more important to me than a paycheque. I didn’t go into journalism to lie or to advertise for a country, I’m not paid for that,” she insists.
Selon le premier <l1>sondage</l1> canadi: According to the first Canadian <l1>survey</l1> on online hate directed at journalists, conducted by Ipsos in 2021, 31% of them admit to having scaled back coverage of certain subjects after being harassed, 23% say they withhold certain information, and 15% acknowledge having abandoned story ideas. These figures offer a glimpse of the harmful effects the strategy adopted by Honest Reporting Canada has on the profession.
« Les directeurs disent tout le temps qu: “Managers are always saying they don’t want to deal with hundreds of emails, which invariably happens in this kind of situation – and HRC knows that very well when it acts this way,” says Samira Mohyeddin. “What happens is that you end up not pitching certain stories. You end up not pitching certain subjects because you figure they don’t want to deal with the emails, and you also don’t want to be seen as the journalist who’s always a headache. I never thought in those terms, I didn’t care, but I know that’s what happens to a lot of journalists.” “I really get the impression that executives worry a lot about what people will say and sacrifice the truth on the altar of fairness when it comes to Israel and Palestine,” she continues. “It’s obvious!”
Interrogé sur ce cas précis, Chuck Thomp: Asked about this specific case, Chuck Thompson, CBC’s director of public affairs, said the following: “The ombudsman’s work is independent of CBC News, which respects his opinion and has no comment on his reviews. CBC News’s correction process does not depend on criticism or correction requests made by anyone. If we learn and confirm that an error exists on our platforms, we correct it. However, if a person or organization claims that an error exists and, after verification, we determine there is no error, we simply tell the complainants that there is nothing to correct. There is no negotiation.” As for ombudsman Jack Nagler, he told us he was “not in a position to participate in our report.”
La directrice de l’information de la CBC: CBC’s director of news, Tracy Seeley, answered our question about the pressure exerted by Honest Reporting and the measures in place to defend journalists at a conference organized on August 27, 2024, by the Centre for Free Expression at Toronto Metropolitan University, on the theme “The Battle to Cover the War in Gaza.” “We tell our journalists that they simply need to focus on accuracy and fairness in their reporting and don’t have to worry about the complaints. (...) It’s difficult when people are targeted directly by groups, and I would say that we are still trying to figure out the best way to protect our journalists,” she says.
De 2022-2023 à 2023-2024, le nombre de p: From 2022-2023 to 2023-2024, the number of complaints sent to CBC rose by 45%, according to the annual report published by Jack Nagler last March. “In total, I received 1,882 complaints about some aspect of CBC’s coverage of this subject (the situation between Israel and Gaza, Editor’s note). That is almost 40% of the entire year’s correspondence,” he notes. “The messages I received reveal a deep divide in how Canadians perceive the events and CBC’s coverage. About 55% of the complaints held that CBC was unfair to Israel,” the ombudsman explains.
Face à ces témoignages, face à l’attitud: Given these accounts, and given the attitude of some newsrooms that appear to be struggling in the face of pressure from Honest Reporting Canada, what is the position of the federations and organizations that represent the profession?

À l’ACJ, Brent Jolly assure plancher sur: At the CAJ, Brent Jolly says he is working on the issue: “Right now I’m looking at upgrading digital security so that journalists are protected. The goal is for us to be ready to face these problems in 2025, which is going to be a busy election year, and so a year with a lot of pressure. If we’re not prepared to meet these challenges, then I will have failed at my job.” That is the promise he has made to the entire profession.
Vue d’Israël, la situation inquiète égal: Seen from Israel, the situation is also worrying some media figures. Gideon Levy, an Israeli journalist and author, answers our question about Honest Reporting Canada from Tel Aviv without hesitation: “The Israeli and Jewish propaganda system made a very sophisticated and strategic decision a few years ago – this didn’t just start – to label any criticism of Israel or of the occupation as antisemitic.
